sections.overview: The mugger, or marsh crocodile, is a broad-snouted crocodilian native to South Asia and eastern Iran. It occupies freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, including reservoirs and irrigation waters. This adaptable predator persists in both protected wetlands and human-altered waterways.
sections.identification: Males usually stay below 3.5 m; females average 2.5–3 m, though exceptional individuals approach 5 m. The mugger has the broadest snout in Crocodylus. Adults are grey-brown; young have lighter colouring and dark bands. Its muscular tail drives swimming, and sturdy limbs support movement on land. Crocodilians can also lift the body into a high walk, though fast gaits are poorly documented for this species. Hatchlings measure about 25–27 cm. The Wildlife Institute of India reports that a large adult male may reach 4.5 m and 450 kg; these are upper-end values, not typical adult size. A reliable female mass range or body-width measurement was not found.
sections.habitat: Muggers inhabit freshwater rivers, lakes, marshes and ponds, often using deeper pools with sandy banks and dense riverside cover. They also occupy reservoirs, irrigation canals and aquaculture ponds; some enter brackish lagoons. This flexibility allows use of human-made waters, but can bring crocodiles near fishing and farming communities.
sections.diet: Muggers are opportunistic carnivores whose diet changes with size. Young take insects, crustaceans and small fish; adults eat fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Deer and buffalo are occasional large prey, not a routine meal for every crocodile. Local feeding reflects available prey and body size; individuals have also been seen corralling fish.
sections.behavior: As ectotherms, muggers warm by basking and cool by entering water or shade. Individuals dig bank burrows that buffer harsh heat and cold; underground temperatures change more slowly than surface air. During prolonged hot, dry spells, a mugger may aestivate—remain inactive in its burrow—then travel overland when seeking permanent water. Such treks can cross roads and railways.
sections.reproduction: Females lay 10–30 eggs in a hole nest, often in sandy bank soil; some nests sit beside or inside burrows. Dry-season laying varies geographically. Eggs incubate for about 55–75 days. Temperature affects sex: controlled experiments yielded all females at 28–31 °C and all males at 32.5 °C, with both sexes at intermediate temperatures. The female guards the nest and may help hatchlings emerge and carry them to water; field observations document such care, but its duration and effect on survival remain uncertain. Captive double clutches have not been documented in the wild.
sections.ecology: As a generalist predator, the mugger links aquatic and terrestrial prey in wetland food webs; its eggs and young are also eaten by other animals. In the Chambal River, a 2024 study found increasing mugger numbers and occupancy in a sanctuary established for gharial recovery. Researchers flagged possible competition with this more habitat-specialised crocodilian as a local management concern, not a proven species-wide effect.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment dated 30 June 2009 and published in 2013 classified the mugger as Vulnerable (A2cd). The IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group estimated over 20,000 adults in its 2025 action plan. Habitat loss, fishing nets, egg collection, persecution and transport deaths remain documented threats. A 2008–2010 survey near Vadodara documented crocodile rescues and relocation after human encounters, illustrating the need for local coexistence measures.
